description:
Wesam Saad approaches free will by distinguishing the person from the faculty of choosing. After reviewing the preceding salvation studies, he defines will as choosing to act, rather than the action itself. His account of the person brings together mind, affections and will within the heart, alongside the continuing flesh. Regeneration changes the heart’s disposition rather than adding a new faculty. He contrasts the old heart’s resistance to God with the renewed heart’s desire for Christ, while retaining the believer’s ongoing struggle with the flesh. These distinctions provide the groundwork for his explanation of choice rather than an immediate yes-or-no answer to an undefined term.

Saad argues that the will follows the person’s strongest desire, and that desires are shaped through the mind. He therefore distinguishes a free person acting from their own inclinations from a will operating independently of that person. A table separates ordinary choices from choices directed towards God and distinguishes possessing faculties from moral ability. Within his terminology, unbelievers remain responsible while lacking a desire to honour God; believers have a new disposition yet still face sinful options through the flesh. Scripture and the renewal of the mind receive practical emphasis. The meeting ends with questions about a professing believer’s weak desires and disability, both carried into the following session.
scripture: 1 Peter 2:11 — identified quotation; spoken chapter uncertain
Renewal of the mind — exact passage not stated

questions.question: What distinction does he make between willing and acting?
questions.answer: Saad defines will as choosing an action, not the action itself. He argues that the phrase free will must be clarified before people debate whether they possess it. The discussion therefore begins by identifying the faculty being considered rather than assuming everyone means the same thing.

questions.question: How does he describe the faculties of the heart?
questions.answer: Saad identifies mind, affections and will as aspects of the inner person, while distinguishing the flesh and its desires. His diagram is a theological explanation of personhood used in the study. It provides the framework for discussing how thoughts, desires and choices relate, rather than a clinical assessment of an individual.

questions.question: What does he say changes in regeneration?
questions.answer: Saad says the faculties remain but their disposition changes: the renewed heart thinks towards Christ, loves him and seeks him. The flesh remains, with its continuing sinful desires. He therefore does not present regeneration as removing every conflict or making the believer incapable of a sinful action.

questions.question: How does desire relate to choice in his explanation?
questions.answer: Saad argues that the strongest desire issues in the choice and that the mind influences the development of desire. He uses this to explain why the will is not an independent faculty detached from the person. This reports his philosophical and theological account, rather than a universal clinical explanation of every human action.

questions.question: How can he say the person is free while the will is bound?
questions.answer: Within Saad’s terminology, the person chooses from their own desires rather than being a puppet. The will remains subject to that person and those desires, not an autonomous power operating separately. His distinction concerns the whole person and one faculty of the person, so the two statements use different senses of freedom.

questions.question: What does he mean by capacity and ability?
questions.answer: Saad uses capacity for possessing the relevant faculties and ability for the moral condition of desire in relation to God. He argues that possessing mind, affection and will does not itself supply a desire to honour God. These are his definitions for the theological discussion, rather than a general legal or medical test of capacity.

questions.question: Why does he maintain responsibility despite moral inability?
questions.answer: Saad locates the inability in an unwilling disposition towards God rather than in the absence of a faculty believers uniquely possess. On that account, the person chooses what they desire and remains accountable. The answer follows his theological reasoning without turning his illustrative scenarios into real-world legal judgments.

questions.question: Why distinguish ordinary choices from God-directed choices?
questions.answer: Saad’s table separates everyday options from the spiritual motive of honouring God. He argues that an unbeliever can choose among ordinary actions while lacking the right disposition towards God. For believers, the new heart opens God-honouring possibilities even though sinful choices remain through the flesh.

questions.question: Why does he emphasise Scripture and the renewal of the mind?
questions.answer: Saad connects the mind with the formation of affections and subsequent choices. He therefore urges attention to Scripture, meditation and teaching that addresses the mind. In his application, this serves growing desire for what pleases God, rather than merely accumulating information without regard to the heart.

questions.question: Which questions are left for the companion session?
questions.answer: The closing questions concern a professing believer who reports little desire for God and the case of someone with a disability. Saad postpones both rather than issuing a complete answer here. The first session should therefore not be used alone to diagnose either an individual’s salvation or a disabled person’s moral standing.
